title: KV backpressure & scheduler heuristics notes
content:
Purpose / motivation:
- Rough labbook for experiments investigating intermittent tail-latency spikes that correlate with heavy KV-cache operations and scheduler decisions. Goal: identify lightweight scheduler heuristics to reduce 99.9th latency regressions for mixed-length workloads (short chat turns + occasional long context).

Background / hypothesis summary:
- Observed problem: under mixed traffic (most reqs seq_len 64–128, occasional seq_len 2048), we see periodic micro-stalls (~10–80ms extra) that cause downstream request timeouts.
- Initial signal: nvprof traces + NVTX show kernel queue flushing and repeated small allocations during the long-context requests.
- Working hypothesis: when long requests evict or preempt KV pages, scheduler admits new short requests into the same worker which triggers inefficient kernel selection (fused-op vs unfused) and causes KV contention + extra host->device synchronization.
- Secondary hypothesis: our current coalescing window and batcher ticketing is blind to KV load; it uses only waiting time/slot count. Need a KV-awareness signal and quick heuristics to reduce switching.

Experiment matrix (what we ran):
- Baseline: current scheduler (coalesce_window_ms=4, max_batch=8), runtime compiled kernels include fused-attn (default) and paged-attn fallback. 2000 req/s mixed distribution (p_short=0.9).
- Experiment A: increase coalesce_window_ms to 8 (more batching for short requests).
- Experiment B: enable "kv-affinity" heuristic: prefer placing consecutive requests that reuse same cache page on same worker (cheap sticky ticketing).
- Experiment C: gate fused-op selection: prefer unfused/paged-attn when pending KV writes exceed threshold (deferred-fusion).
- Experiment D: dynamic-ticketing: allow preemptive pause of admitting new short requests while long request in flight for up to N ms (N=6).

Workload generator notes (how to reproduce):
- Synthetic harness: tools/bench/mix_runner.py --qps 2000 --dist short:0.9,long:0.1 --short-len 64 --long-len 2048 --temp 0.2 --shuffle 1000
- Worker config snapshot used: runtime:v1.39, kernel-set:opt-a, flash-disabled=false, paged-threshold=1024
- Profiling flags: RUNTIME_NVTX=1 TRACE_KERNEL_IDS=1 PERF_SAMPLING=off

Key observations (numbers are med/95/99/999 latencies in ms for generation-only latency; tail numbers noisy so multiple runs):
- Baseline: med 6.1 / p95 22.8 / p99 47.9 / p999 92.1 (spikes coincide with long requests start/end)
- A (wider coalescing): med 7.3 / p95 19.9 / p99 45.5 / p999 88.0 -> slightly better p95 but not p999 (bigger batches increased med a touch)
- B (kv-affinity): med 6.5 / p95 18.5 / p99 39.8 / p999 56.6 -> substantial p999 improvement
- C (deferred-fusion): med 6.2 / p95 19.0 / p99 42.3 / p999 59.3 -> improved p99 but not as strong as kv-affinity for p999
- D (preemptive pause N=6ms): med 6.9 / p95 17.7 / p99 37.1 / p999 52.0 -> best p999, slightly higher med

Micro-trace analysis (selected NVTX stack snippets around a 999 spike):
- Trace shows a long-request performing KV write sequence (host->device memcpy small fragments) interleaved with several short request kernels that trigger fused-attn path requiring different scratchspace.
- Kernel queue snapshot: worker W3 had 3 short request kernels queued which forced kernel launches that clobbered a scratch allocator used by the long request, leading to synchronization and kernel re-setup.
- Observed repeated device memset (~2–6KB) calls that appear tied to our small-allocation branch in the fused op path when sequence lengths vary.

What seemed to help and why (qualitative):
- KV-affinity (B): reduces interleaving of requests touching same cache pages; it keeps page-resident state local to a worker and reduces cross-worker eviction/rehydration. This avoids repeated device memcpys and kernel rebinds.
- Preemptive pause (D): simple throttle that prevents admitting new short jobs while long job is inside critical KV commit window. This eliminates the pathological interleaving at cost of slightly increased median for short calls.
- Deferred fusion (C): avoids expensive fused-kernel path when heavy KV ops are present; reduced scratch churn but tradeoff with throughput for mostly-long workloads.

Rejected/negative ideas we tried quickly:
- Aggressive page pinning (pin all KV pages to GPU): reduced swaps but caused memory pressure and OOMs during concurrent bursts. Not viable without dynamic eviction policy.
- Global per-GPU lock around KV operations: solved tail but collapsed throughput (serialized everything).

Implementation sketch for a lightweight heuristic (prototype):
- Maintain per-worker KV-touch-count (atomic counter updated on any KV read/write for request).
- When accepting a new request, check: if there exists an active long-request (kv-touch-count > LONG_THRESHOLD) on that worker, and incoming request is short, then either:
  a) prefer route to different worker (if capacity available)
  b) if no spare worker, delay admit for up to PAUSE_MS (configurable) before admitting to same worker
- Fallback: if route fails repeatedly, fall back to deferred-fusion kernel (so short request can progress without scratch rebind).
- Config knobs: LONG_THRESHOLD (pages touched), PAUSE_MS, affinity-window-ms, deferred-fusion-bias (0..1)

Prototype notes:
- Implemented minimal counters + ticket check in 1-file change to scheduler (patch linked_artifact PR).
- Lightweight (O(1) check) and empirically low overhead in hot path.
- Danger: increased routing churn + jitter if many long requests; mitigation: hysteresis (only apply after M long requests within window).

Open questions / next runs:
- How does this behave under multi-tenant Dedicated clusters where worker isolation is different? Need tests with 4x tenants.
- Are there degenerate cases where kv-affinity causes hotspotting across workers? Need heatmap of page ownership.
- Should the scheduler expose a KV-load metric in tracing/console (observable)? Likely yes — add metric: kv_pages_active_per_worker and kv_evictions/sec.
- Explore combining deferred-fusion + kv-affinity: allow short requests to proceed on unfused path when affinity fails.

Immediate next steps (actionable):
- (Marco) Run 12-hour soak with kv-affinity enabled on canary pool (pool:canary-west-2-small). Collect p999 distribution and eviction metrics. (owner: Marco)
- (Lena) Add two new tracing counters (kv_pages_active, kv_evictions) and dashboard tile. (owner: Lena)
- (Tomás) Evaluate memory pressure tradeoffs for pinned pages with bounded pin budget (policy: pin up to P pages per-worker). (owner: Tomás)
- Roll a simple safety toggle behind feature-flag: runtime.scheduler.kv_heuristics = off/on with default off.

Notes to reviewers:
- This doc is intentionally informal; contains experiment configs and quick numbers. If promising, convert to a formal runbook with exact commands and raw CSVs attached.
- PR with prototype scheduling check: GH PR linked above; patch is small but touches hot path — needs careful perf microbench.

Appendix: quick command snippets used
- run bench: python tools/bench/mix_runner.py --qps 2000 --dist short:0.9,long:0.1 --short-len 64 --long-len 2048 
- start runtime with nvtx: RUNTIME_NVTX=1 ./bazel-bin/runtime/main --config canary-west-2-small
- collect nvprof sample (short run): sudo nvprof --profile-child-processes --print-gpu-trace -o nvtrace.nvvp /path/to/worker_binary

Raw kernel snippet (example NVTX timeline excerpt):
- [t=0ms] accept(short) -> launch fused-attn seq=64 -> kernel K1 (fused)
- [t=1ms] accept(long) -> allocate scratch -> memcpy small frag -> kernel K2 (paged-attn)
- [t=1.6ms] short requests launched on same GPU -> K3 tries to reuse scratch -> kernel preemption -> device sync
- Sync cost observed ~6–22ms depending on scratch rebind path

End of labbook entry.

[hand-off: convert to a formal runbook if canary soak shows >40% reduction in p999.]
